Guided Inquiry

1 · Reading a spacetime diagram

Let’s get our bearings first. This diagram plots time upward as ct and space sideways as x, and c = 1 in these units, so a light ray draws a line at exactly 45° — those are the dashed yellow diagonals. A single point is an event: one place at one moment. A continuous line is a worldline: the whole history of one object.

2 · Two histories

Let’s put that to work. Picture a marble sitting at rest at x = 0 while an hour passes, and a second marble travelling steadily to the right. What do you think their two worldlines look like on this diagram?

Take a look — both worldlines are now drawn: the vertical one is at rest, and the leaning one carries v/c = +0.50.

3 · Equal heights

Now look at the two events on the diagram. E1 and E2 sit at the same height above the x axis, but at different x. What do you think equal height tells you about them?

Check the readings: frame S gives cΔt = +0.00 and Δx = +4.00 for this pair.

4 · How far can a worldline lean?

Here’s where it gets interesting. Draw worldlines at several different tilts, and you’ll see each one is labelled with its v/c. What do you think is the significance of that label?

Notice the pattern: the steeper a worldline stands, the slower the object, and the 45° diagonals are light itself.

5 · A 45° separation

One last experiment. Drag E2 until the straight line joining E1 to E2 runs parallel to a dashed 45° diagonal. Which statement about the two events do you think is then true?

Try it both ways: lean the joining line inside 45° and Δs² turns negative; lean it outside and Δs² turns positive.

The Physics

Spacetime diagrams · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A spacetime diagram plots time upward and space sideways, so one moment at one place becomes a dot and a whole history becomes a line. This sim lets you place two events, draw worldlines, and read what frame S assigns to the pair.

What you'll learn

  • How an event and a worldline are drawn on a diagram of ct against x.
  • How the slope of a worldline relates to the speed it stands for.
  • How the readings Δx, cΔt and Δs² follow from where E1 and E2 sit.
  • How the sign of Δs² relates to the way the two events are joined.
Time upward (as ct), space sideways (x), and two events with the dashed 45° lines through the origin.

What's on screen

  • E1 and E2 (teal, rose): the events you drag, labelled (ct, x).
  • Dashed yellow diagonals: 45° lines through the origin; with c = 1, the paths of light.
  • Dotted teal lines (Detail 2): from each event to both axes.
  • Amber legs (Detail 3): the two parts of the separation.
  • Worldlines you draw, each labelled with its v/c.
  • Frame S panel: Δx, cΔt and Δs², signed.
See itStart from the opening picture. Watch for: E1 (teal) and E2 (rose), each labelled with its (ct, x), and the dashed yellow lines crossing at the origin.

03

What a dot is, and what its numbers mean

A dot is an event: one place at one moment, such as a flash or a collision. It is not an object and not a path.

  • Both axes are lengths. Multiplying time by c turns it into a distance, so ct and x share one unit. The sim sets c = 1: one unit of ct is the time light takes to cross one unit of x.
  • A frame is a labelling rule. It gives every event a pair (ct, x). Frame S is the one drawn here, and its axes stay fixed. Another frame would label the same event with different numbers; the labels belong to the frame, the event does not.
  • Equal ct, equal x. Two events with the same ct are at the same moment in frame S. Two with the same x are at the same place in frame S.
One second of ct is one light-second of distance, about 3.0 × 10⁸ m.
See itTurn on Detail 2 for the current pair. Watch for: dotted teal lines from each dot to the ct axis and the x axis, ending at the two numbers in its label.
04

A worldline is a history

A worldline is the whole history of one object drawn as one line: all its events in order. Nothing on the diagram moves; the picture shows the motion.

  • At rest is vertical. An object that stays put still advances in ct, so its worldline runs straight up.
  • Motion tilts it. If x advances with ct, the line leans. The sim labels it v/c = Δx / Δ(ct), signed: positive leans right.
  • Steeper means slower. The slope drawn is Δ(ct)/Δx = 1/(v/c), so a nearly vertical line is a slow object.
  • The 45° lines are light. They carry v/c = ±1. A line flatter than 45° would read |v/c| > 1. The tool lets you draw one, but no particle or signal has such a worldline.
At rest (teal), moving at v/c = +0.50 (blue), light (dashed). Shaded: slopes nothing can have.
See itDraw three worldlines with different tilts. Watch for: the vertical line labelled v/c = +0.00, the leaning ones labelled larger values, and all of them steeper than the dashed 45° lines.
05

Separating two events

In frame S, the pair E1, E2 is separated by a time part and a space part, both signed (E2 minus E1). Together they give the interval Δs².

In Δs² the time part carries the minus sign.
x₁ ct₁ x₂ ct₂

These sliders are E1 and E2: they move the events in the sim too.

  • Δs² is neither a distance nor a time. It is the one combination of the two that every inertial frame agrees on, which is why it has a name.
  • Detail 3 draws it: the vertical leg is cΔt, the horizontal leg is Δx.
See itTurn on Detail 3 for a sample pair. Watch for: the amber legs labelled Δx and cΔt, and the same two numbers, with Δs² = −5, in the card.
06

The sign of Δs² sorts every pair

  • Δs² < 0, timelike. The time part wins; the joining line is steeper than 45°. Something slower than light can be at both events, so the earlier can cause the later. A negative value is a result, not an error.
  • Δs² = 0, null. The joining line is exactly 45°: light from the earlier event arrives at the later one.
  • Δs² > 0, spacelike. The space part wins; the line is flatter than 45°. No signal joins the pair, and some frame sees the two events at the same time.
  • Frames split the interval differently between time and space, but they agree on Δs², so they agree on its sign.
Timelike pairs give Δs² < 0, null pairs 0, spacelike pairs Δs² > 0.
See itMove E2 through three positions around E1. Watch for: Δs² reading negative, then +0.00, then positive.
07

Where it matters

  • A solar flare and its light arriving at Earth. The Sun is 1 AU, about 499 light-seconds (8 min 19 s), away. The pair has Δx = cΔt = 499 light-seconds, so Δs² = 0: null, and sunlight's worldline is the 45° line itself.
  • "Now" here and "now" at Proxima Centauri. With Δx = 4.25 ly and cΔt = 0 in frame S, Δs² ≈ +18 ly²: spacelike. No signal can connect those two events.
  • Everyday life. A handclap and a blink 1 ms later, 1 m apart, have cΔt ≈ 300 km against Δx = 1 m: very timelike. Light crosses 1 m in about 3.3 ns, which is why the 45° limit is never noticed at a desk.
Two real pairs of events, drawn like the sim's diagram.
Go deeper: what Δs² measures
  • For a timelike pair, √(−Δs²) is c times the time recorded by a clock that moves at constant velocity and is present at both events: the proper time (Lecture 9).
  • For a spacelike pair, √Δs² is the distance between the events in the frame where they are simultaneous.
08

Summary

In one line. A frame labels each event with (ct, x). The interval Δs² = −(cΔt)² + (Δx)² is the same in every inertial frame, and its sign says what can join the two events: slower-than-light travel, light, or nothing.

Key points

  • A dot is an event; its coordinates are labels from a frame.
  • A worldline is a history: vertical at rest, tilting with speed.
  • With c = 1, light draws the 45° lines and v/c = Δx / Δ(ct).
  • In this sim Δs² is negative for timelike pairs, zero for null, positive for spacelike.

Common mix-ups

  • "An object at rest is a point." It still advances in ct, so its worldline is vertical.
  • "Steeper means faster." The slope drawn is 1/(v/c), so steeper means slower.
  • "Equal height means simultaneous for everyone." Equal ct means simultaneous in frame S; another frame can disagree for events at different x.

Things to try on your own

  • Turn on Detail 3 and drag E2 until the pair lies along a dashed diagonal. Read Δs².
  • Set Δx = 3 and cΔt = 1, then swap the two values. Compare the signs of Δs².
  • Draw a steep and a flat worldline with ✎ Add worldline and compare their v/c labels.
